text: Who stated that “artificial intelligence is the science of making machines do things that would require intelligence if done by men”?
choice_a: Allen Newell
choice_b: John McCarthy
choice_c: Marvin Minsky
choice_d: Kevin Warwick
clue: Think of the MIT AI researcher known for studying common-sense intelligence.

text: Who coined the phrase “Artificial Intelligence” for the 1956 Dartmouth conference?
choice_a: Marvin Minsky
choice_b: Allen Newell
choice_c: John McCarthy
choice_d: Horvitz
clue: Recall the Dartmouth organizer also associated with the Lisp programming language.

text: Who originally formulated the IQ test in 1904 to help identify kids who might struggle in a normal school environment?
choice_a: Frances Galton
choice_b: Alfred Binet
choice_c: Cyril Burt
choice_d: John Loehlin
clue: Think of the French psychologist whose work focused on assessing schoolchildren.

text: According to Kevin Warwick’s Artificial Intelligence: The Basics, what was the primary reason for the loss of AI research funding during the 1970s?
choice_a: Highly optimistic claims from 1960s that failed to produce the promised results.
choice_b: A conflict in ideas between researchers as to how AI should be developed.
choice_c: Limited computing power.
choice_d: Lack of aspiring researchers in the field due to its complexity and cost.
clue: Compare what researchers promised with what their systems could actually deliver.

text: Which statement best expresses Marvin Minsky’s definition of artificial intelligence?
choice_a: Machines that only store knowledge
choice_b: Machines doing tasks that require human intelligence
choice_c: Machines used only for games
choice_d: Machines with no knowledge
clue: Focus on the kind of task being performed, rather than a particular application.

text: Based on Allen Newell's Unified Theories of Cognition, how does a system accurately demonstrate "perfect intelligence"?
choice_a: By defining problem boundaries
choice_b: By bringing all the knowledge it has at its disposal to bear in the solution of a problem
choice_c: By copying human common sense
choice_d: By having high IQ
clue: Consider whether the system uses everything it knows when tackling a problem.

text: A school describes a student’s entire intelligence using only one IQ score. What concern from the passage applies?
choice_a: IQ is only for researchers
choice_b: One score may not show all abilities
choice_c: Students cannot take IQ tests
choice_d: Intelligence cannot be measured
clue: Think about whether one measurement can capture many different kinds of ability.

text: You are testing a brand new robot to see if it actually possesses "common-sense knowledge" according to Marvin Minsky's standards. Which task should you assign it to prove this?
choice_a: Assemble a car part
choice_b: Fill a glass with water
choice_c: Beat a human at chess
choice_d: Solve a differential equation
clue: Look for an everyday activity that requires practical understanding of the physical world.

text: Which application area of artificial intelligence would be useful for making a chatbot that can communicate in a user's dialect?
choice_a: Expert Systems
choice_b: Vision and Speech
choice_c: Natural Language Processing (NLP)
choice_d: Problem Solving
clue: Focus on understanding and producing human language.

text: How does Minsky’s definition of AI differ from Newell’s?
choice_a: Newell believed AI is the ability of a machine to be physically fit while Minsky defined AI as the ability to think critically.
choice_b: Marvin Minsky defined AI as machines doing tasks that require human intelligence, while Newell focused on copying human intelligence.
choice_c: Minsky focused on machines doing tasks that require human intelligence, while Newell saw intelligence as approximating knowledge-level systems to achieve goals.
choice_d: They both believe AI is the new meta.
clue: Compare a definition based on human tasks with one based on knowledge and goals.

text: Why can passing the Turing Test still be questioned as proof of intelligence?
choice_a: It depends on human judgement
choice_b: It measures only memory
choice_c: It ignores machine behavior
choice_d: It tests only speed
clue: Consider who decides whether the machine sounds intelligent.

text: You test a new chatbot that reads your English prompts perfectly. But it only replies in a raw binary code. Which specific NLP component is missing?
choice_a: Voice Recognition
choice_b: Natural Language Generation
choice_c: Heuristic algorithm
choice_d: Natural Language Understanding
clue: The input is understood; think about the stage that creates a readable response.

text: Evaluate the following options and choose the one that best states the advantage of AI compared with human capabilities in medical diagnostics.
choice_a: AI is useful in complementing human expertise because it can analyze drug interactions without fatigue, while humans provide clinical judgment.
choice_b: AI can totally replace humans because they can easily learn medications.
choice_c: It is still too early to apply AI in medical diagnostics.
choice_d: AI does not make mistakes, unlike humans.
clue: Look for an option where computational strengths support professional judgment.

text: According to John McCarthy’s view, which AI design should be considered better?
choice_a: One that closely copies human thinking
choice_b: One that solves problems effectively in its own way
choice_c: One that imitates human conversation
choice_d: One that behaves exactly like a person
clue: Judge the result achieved rather than how closely the method resembles human thinking.

text: Many computer scientists argue that the Turing Test is a fundamentally flawed measurement. Which specific assumption do these critics challenge to justify rejecting the test?
choice_a: Code limits math speed
choice_b: Interrogators are easily fooled
choice_c: It strictly compares behavior
choice_d: The physical rooms isolate signals
clue: Consider whether observable conversation alone establishes what happens inside a system.

text: Choose the option that best synthesizes why AI struggled during its winter age and how it was able to recover.
choice_a: The people feared that AI might take over and rule everything but succeeding studies showed no definitive proof of this happening which allowed the research to continue.
choice_b: There was no noticeable improvement in the AI research so most researchers abandoned it, however a decade later, a human-like robot was built which sparked new hope for the field.
choice_c: Lack of computing power, small data and vocabulary, and over-expectations during the 1960s resulted in a lack of AI research funding, but it was able to recover only after AI researchers stopped making it exactly imitate the human brain and instead focused it on certain domains.
choice_d: AI struggled due to multiple bugs in its codebase but it has learned on its own mistakes and revived itself.
clue: Connect research expectations, practical limitations and a later narrowing of the problems being tackled.

text: Choose the option that best synthesizes the change in thinking about how AI should be developed.
choice_a: AI should copy human thinking before attempting any problem.
choice_b: AI should focus on human behavior rather than successful results.
choice_c: AI could solve problems in its own way instead of exactly copying human intelligence.
choice_d: AI development should avoid using abilities that differ from humans.
clue: Consider whether useful intelligent behavior requires reproducing the human thinking process.

text: Your team wants to develop an intelligent emergency response system. The system should understand emergency calls, determine the type of emergency, and recommend the best route for responders. Which combination of AI application areas would best achieve this goal?
choice_a: Game playing + Robotics
choice_b: Vision system + Voice system
choice_c: Natural Language Processing + Expert Systems + Problem Solving
choice_d: Speech recognition only
clue: Break the task into understanding the caller, applying specialist knowledge and planning a route.

text: What does problem-solving involve?
choice_a: Moving from an initial situation to a goal using resources.
choice_b: Reducing a composite situation into easier sub-problems.
choice_c: Using an internal knowledge base to constrain solutions.
choice_d: Guaranteeing a 100% correct transition to a goal state.
clue: Think about what separates the starting situation from the desired outcome.

text: In state space representation, what does the term "state" exactly define?
choice_a: A procedural rule
choice_b: The position at a certain time
choice_c: A global database
choice_d: An operator limit
clue: Imagine taking a snapshot of the problem while a search is in progress.

text: According to Polya, an important step in understanding a problem is isolation of principal parts. What are these?
choice_a: the data, the conditions, and the solutions
choice_b: the conditions, the boundaries, and the solutions
choice_c: the data, the conditions, and the unknowns
choice_d: the data, the unknowns, and the solutions
clue: Separate what is given, what must hold and what must be found.

text: Which statement best explains the difference between an algorithm and a heuristic?
choice_a: Algorithms guarantee a 100% correct solution, while heuristics select likely paths without guarantees.
choice_b: Algorithms strictly fit the Human Window, while heuristics guarantee a solution.
choice_c: Algorithms evaluate every node, while heuristics rely on backward chaining.
choice_d: Algorithms use exhaustive enumeration, while heuristics use problem reduction.
clue: Compare a prescribed solution procedure with a rule that guides promising choices.

text: A production system has the characteristics of a monotonic production system and also satisfies the partially commutative condition. Based on these characteristics, which type of production system is being described?
choice_a: Monotonic Production System
choice_b: Non-Monotonic Production System
choice_c: Commutative Law Based Production System
choice_d: Partially Commutative Production System
clue: Look for the system type that combines both properties named in the question.

text: Which of the following best describes the primary purpose of a production system in artificial intelligence?
choice_a: To execute hardware tasks automatically without the need for an algorithm or database.
choice_b: To structure problem-solving by separating domain knowledge from the control mechanism that executes those rules.
choice_c: To ensure the system does not make mistakes by eliminating heuristics.
choice_d: To translate natural language queries into machine code without the use of logic.
clue: Consider the relationship between stored rules and the mechanism that chooses and applies them.

text: An AI starts at one condition, applies allowed actions, and continues until it reaches a desired condition. Which method is being used?
choice_a: Problem analysis
choice_b: State Space Search
choice_c: Problem reduction
choice_d: Conflict resolution
clue: Imagine possible situations connected by the actions that move between them.

text: A group of students needs to calculate the factorial of a number. They decide to solve the problem by having a function repeatedly call itself with a smaller value until it reaches 1. Which problem-solving technique are the students applying?
choice_a: Exhaustive enumeration
choice_b: Backward chaining
choice_c: Recursion
choice_d: Generate and Test
clue: Look at how the function tackles a smaller instance of its own task.

text: A politician was asked how to solve urban flooding. He answered: “We will simply collect all the floodwater and save it to use during dry seasons.” Which criterion of Polya’s Human Window was violated, and why?
choice_a: Grain Size – because it contains many sub-steps.
choice_b: Executability – it lacks resources, infrastructure, and realistic steps needed to carry it out.
choice_c: Comprehensibility – the idea is too complex for regular people.
choice_d: Representation – the problem lacks a proper search tree structure.
clue: Ask whether the proposed action can actually be carried out with the available means.

text: Critique the argument made by Hubert Dreyfus regarding expert systems vs. human expertise. What core distinction does he highlight to challenge the traditional knowledge representation approach?
choice_a: Experts rely on symbolic manipulation and explicit reasoning, where novices act on instincts.
choice_b: Experts have compiled out all declarative knowledge, making them less accurate than knowledge-based systems.
choice_c: Novices figure out actions through deliberate reasoning, whereas experts recognize patterns and react without step-by-step symbolic reasoning.
choice_d: Expert performance is limited because human brains cannot compute predicate logic at runtime.
clue: Compare a beginner working through rules with an expert recognizing a familiar situation.

text: Two programs give the same answer, but only one explicitly stores facts that it reasons with. What mainly distinguishes the second program?
choice_a: It produces more accurate outputs
choice_b: It uses an explicit knowledge base
choice_c: It follows fewer instructions
choice_d: It performs calculations faster
clue: Focus on how facts are represented and used, rather than whether the final answers match.

text: When analyzing an AI system, how does Allen Newell's "knowledge level" fundamentally differ from the "symbol level"?
choice_a: The knowledge level focuses exclusively on computational data structures.
choice_b: The knowledge level describes what an agent knows and its goals, while the symbol level describes how that knowledge is represented and processed.
choice_c: The knowledge level strictly tests the execution speed of algorithms.
choice_d: The knowledge level maps out the physical hardware limits.
clue: Compare describing what an agent knows and wants with describing its internal implementation.

text: When deciding whether to replace a traditional DBMS with a knowledge-based system, which choice highlights the primary tradeoff and potential risk of this change?
choice_a: The KBS will require clerical personnel rather than domain experts for routine updates, which increases human error.
choice_b: The KBS requires much more computational power and expertise to manage logical inferences, whereas the DBMS excels at rapid, direct retrieval of data.
choice_c: The DBMS is incapable of storing facts about single objects, whereas the KBS can only operate on single instances.
choice_d: The KBS will drastically increase data storage requirements because its knowledge base must be larger than a standard database.
clue: Consider the extra reasoning work involved when stored facts must support new conclusions.

text: A developer expects an AI system’s knowledge to be updated often and reused for different conclusions. Which representation should the developer choose?
choice_a: Procedural, because each action is already specified
choice_b: Procedural, because rules are harder to modify
choice_c: Declarative, because knowledge can be reused and easily changed
choice_d: Declarative, because it does not require inference
clue: Think about keeping statements of knowledge separate from the steps that use them.

text: When designing an inference engine, why would a developer choose to implement backward chaining instead of forward chaining?
choice_a: Because it solves open-ended design and planning problems.
choice_b: Because it is best suited for applications where the possible conclusions are limited and well-defined.
choice_c: Because it moves strictly from available facts to an open-ended goal.
choice_d: Because it requires continuous external sensor input to function.
clue: Consider starting with a candidate conclusion and checking the evidence needed to support it.

text: You are building an automated customer service chatbot using a Frame architecture. You need the system to immediately alert a supervisor whenever a customer mentions an urgent safety issue. Which integration best solves the requirement?
choice_a: Place an “if-added” attached procedure inside a frame slot that triggers an external alert when a safety keyword is detected.
choice_b: Convert the frame into a semantic network every time a safety keyword is detected.
choice_c: Use backward-chaining to delete the customer’s working storage database.
choice_d: Store the safety rules in a decision-tree leaf node so the system does not need a user interface.
clue: Look for a mechanism that reacts immediately when information is added to a slot.

text: A company wants one expert system to apply the same expertise to many different customer cases while reasoning separately about each case. Which arrangement best supports this design?
choice_a: Use the database for reusable expertise and the knowledge base for temporary case facts
choice_b: Use the knowledge base for reusable expertise and the database for the current case
choice_c: Use the inference engine to store expertise and the database to store conclusions
choice_d: Use the knowledge base to store conclusions and the inference engine to store case facts
clue: Separate reusable expertise from the changing facts of an individual customer case.

text: Choose the option that best synthesizes the primary goal of Conceptual Dependency theory.
choice_a: It restricts natural language understanding to strict true or false logic.
choice_b: It extracts knowledge directly from domain experts using structured interviews.
choice_c: It creates a single, language-independent representation of meaning for sentences that mean the same thing.
choice_d: It records stereotyped sequences of events like a bank robbery into a database.
clue: Ask how different sentences or languages could express the same underlying idea.

text: What is the average number of child nodes in a problem-space graph called?
choice_a: Problem depth
choice_b: Admissibility
choice_c: Branching factor
choice_d: Space Complexity
clue: Think about how many branches typically extend from one node.

text: What does the term "Branching Factor" specifically define in a problem space graph?
choice_a: The maximum number of nodes stored in the computer's memory.
choice_b: The length of the shortest path from the initial state to the goal state.
choice_c: The average number of child nodes for a given node.
choice_d: The total amount of time taken to generate new nodes.
clue: Consider what varies at each node, not a fixed limit or total count.

text: What is the space complexity of a breadth-first search?
choice_a: O(b^d) where d is depth and b is branching factor
choice_b: O(bn) where n is total nodes
choice_c: O(b)
clue: Recall that breadth-first search stores every node at each level in memory.

text: What is the fundamental purpose of adding a heuristic function to a search process?
choice_a: To guarantee that the algorithm sequentially searches every single node in the problem space.
choice_b: To evaluate states and estimate which node is most likely closest to the goal state.
choice_c: To convert an informed algorithm into a blind, brute-force search.
choice_d: To randomly generate new domains and physical constraints.
clue: Focus on how promising a state looks, rather than blind exploration.

text: Why can forward search become less directed than backward search?
choice_a: The goal must always be unknown
choice_b: It always searches the deepest branch first
choice_c: It cannot use IF-THEN rules
choice_d: Many rules may apply without specifically leading toward the goal
clue: Consider how many stored rules could fire without aiming at the goal.

text: Which of the following best explains how a beam search operates to control memory usage during a search process?
choice_a: It explores the deepest path first, storing only the path from the root to the current node before backtracking.
choice_b: It expands all successor nodes at each level, but retains only a fixed number of the most promising states based on a heuristic evaluation.
choice_c: It computes the exact cost function g(n) plus heuristic cost h(n) for every node across the entire search space without discarding any nodes.
choice_d: It evaluates immediate local neighbors and irrevocably moves to the best neighbour without keeping track of alternative paths or previous state.
clue: Think about a heuristic filter that discards all but the top candidates.

text: A problem solver knows extra information about which states are more promising and wants to use that knowledge to guide where it searches next. Which approach should it use?
choice_a: Exhaustive search
choice_b: Heuristic search
choice_c: Binary search
choice_d: Layered search
clue: Look for the approach that uses extra domain knowledge to prioritize states.

text: A group of students is developing a search program to explore a search tree layer by layer, checking all nodes at the current level before expanding deeper to find the shallowest solution. Which search technique are the students applying?
choice_a: Depth-First Search
choice_b: Linear Search
choice_c: Breadth-First Search
choice_d: Binary Search
clue: Think about exploring every node one level before moving deeper.

text: Consider a decision-tree being searched using the upper-left-right binary tree search algorithm. For any subtree root node P with child nodes L (left) and R (right), in what operational order does ulr(P) evaluate these nodes?
choice_a: Evaluate L, then R, then tests P.
choice_b: Evaluate L, then tests P, then evaluates R.
choice_c: Tests P first; if not a solution, recursively searches L, then recursively searches R.
choice_d: Evaluates R first, then recursively searches L, then tests P.
clue: Trace the order: test the root first, then explore left, then right.

text: How does Alpha-Beta pruning fundamentally improve the standard Minimax algorithm?
choice_a: It changes the game into a single-player puzzle.
choice_b: It completely eliminates the combinatorial explosion of states.
choice_c: It cuts the number of game states the system has to examine in half.
choice_d: It replaces the static evaluation function with random guessing.
clue: Think about the states an unpromising branch causes the algorithm to skip.

text: Which of the following best analyzes the core underlying cause of the “horizon effect” in computer game playing programs?
choice_a: The static evaluation function is too low, causing memory buffer overflows before reaching terminal nodes.
choice_b: The program assumes the opponent will make suboptimal moves, leading to incorrect heuristic moves.
choice_c: Fixed search depth limits prevent the program from detecting critical state changes that occur just beyond the maximum evaluated ply.
choice_d: Alpha-Beta pruning incorrectly eliminates optimal branches due to unsorted move generators.
clue: Consider what happens just past the point where the search stops looking.

text: A problem is divided into two types of nodes: one requires all child problems to succeed, while another requires at least one child problem to succeed. What does this reveal?
choice_a: Both nodes are OR-nodes
choice_b: The first is an AND-node and the second an OR-node
choice_c: The first is an OR-node and the second an AND-node
choice_d: Both nodes are terminal nodes
clue: Match ‘succeeds only if all children succeed’ with the right node type.

text: A chess program already uses minimax correctly, but it examines too many states. Which improvement is most appropriate?
choice_a: Add alpha-beta pruning
choice_b: Remove the minimizer
choice_c: Replace evaluation with random choices
choice_d: Expand every branch further
clue: Recall the standard technique for cutting down state examination in minimax.

text: Evaluate the primary drawback of using standard minimax in real-world game environments with human opponents.
choice_a: Minimax assumes the opponent plays optimally to maximize their gain.
choice_b: Minimax cannot evaluate terminal states unless the complete game tree is fully expanded to the leaf nodes.
choice_c: Minimax requires a heuristic evaluation function that remains completely static throughout all depth levels.
choice_d: Minimax fails to operate in two-player zero-sum games where one player is a maximizer and the other is the minimizer.
clue: Think about what minimax assumes regarding how the opponent behaves.

text: When designing a proof-search algorithm, why would a developer purposefully choose backward search instead of forward search?
choice_a: Because the system's axioms have only one input and multiple outputs, making the branching factor smaller in reverse.
choice_b: Because backward search completely ignores the branching factor of the problem space graph.
choice_c: Because the initial state of the environment is entirely unknown.
choice_d: Because forward search requires a strict alpha-beta cut-off to work.
clue: Consider which direction leaves fewer possible paths to follow.

text: Suppose you want to formulate an improved search algorithm that maximizes the number of cut-offs achieved by Alpha-Beta pruning. Which design strategy for node expansion should you construct?
choice_a: Generate and evaluate child nodes in random order so that alpha and beta windows adjust dynamically.
choice_b: Order move generation so that the plausible move generator expands the most promising (“best”) moves first at each level.
choice_c: Expand leaf nodes in reverse order of their static evaluation scores, starting with the worst potential minimizer moves.
choice_d: Disable Alpha-Beta window adjustments until all leaf nodes at depth n have been fully evaluated by the static function.
clue: Think about examining the strongest candidate moves before the weaker ones.

text: You are writing the exact cutoff logic for an Alpha-Beta pruning algorithm. Which condition correctly tells the system to stop exploring a specific branch?
choice_a: The algorithm stops when the upper bound (beta) becomes less than or equal to the lower bound (alpha).
choice_b: The algorithm stops when the maximizing player achieves a positive heuristic score.
choice_c: The algorithm stops when the static evaluation function reaches exactly zero.
choice_d: The algorithm stops when the plausible move generator runs out of memory.
clue: Recall the comparison between the best guaranteed values for each player.

text: A programmer wants to keep the basic idea of moving down a search path, but instead of always taking the first available child, the program should choose the child that appears most promising. Which search design does this create?
choice_a: Breadth-first search
choice_b: Best-first search
choice_c: Ordinary depth-first search
choice_d: Binary search
clue: Think about picking the most promising child instead of the first one.
